introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (headed "One hour 30 minutes" on page 2): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (40 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (50 minutes): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) What is the difference between an energy source and an energy resource.

(ii) What is energy security?

(iii) State two steps Cameroon can take to work towards energy security. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) An **energy source** is the natural origin from which useful energy can be obtained: the Sun, wind, falling water, biomass, fossil fuels, uranium. An **energy resource** is the amount of that source which is actually available and can be exploited with present technology and at an acceptable cost, for example the proven reserves of oil and gas, or the part of the river flow that can be used for hydroelectric power. The source is the origin; the resource is the exploitable stock or potential.

(ii) **Energy security** is the uninterrupted availability of enough energy, at an affordable price and from sustainable, reliable supplies, to meet the needs of a country now and in the future.

(iii) Two steps (with reasons):

1. **Diversify the energy mix** by developing, besides hydroelectricity, other local renewable sources (solar in the sunny north, biomass, wind, small hydro) and natural gas, so that a drought, a breakdown or a price rise affecting one source does not cause a national shortage.
2. **Improve the transmission and distribution grid and energy efficiency** (reduce losses, add storage and interconnections, promote efficient appliances and lamps), so that more of the energy generated actually reaches users and demand grows more slowly than supply.

(Other valid steps: reduce dependence on imported fuel, build strategic fuel reserves, improved cooking stoves and biogas to reduce firewood use.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Draw a block diagram of a nuclear power plant highlighting the energy changes in each block.

(ii) Nuclear fusion is a very popular but non-exploitable source of energy at moment. Explain why it is rather nuclear fission that is used to produce energy. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The diagram is to be **drawn by the candidate**. Model answer: draw five blocks joined by arrows, labelling the energy change in each block.

1. **Reactor core** (fuel rods of uranium-235, moderator, control rods): nuclear energy $\to$ thermal (internal) energy, by controlled chain-reaction fission. The coolant carries the heat away.
2. **Heat exchanger / steam generator**: thermal energy of the hot coolant $\to$ thermal energy of high-pressure steam.
3. **Turbine**: thermal energy of the steam $\to$ kinetic energy of the rotating turbine.
4. **Generator** (alternator): kinetic energy $\to$ electrical energy.
5. **Transformer and transmission lines**: electrical energy at the generator voltage $\to$ electrical energy at high voltage for the grid.

The steam leaving the turbine goes to a **condenser** cooled by water from a river, the sea or a cooling tower, which rejects the waste heat, and the condensed water returns to the steam generator.

(ii) **Fusion** needs the nuclei to come close enough to overcome their electrostatic repulsion, which requires temperatures of about $10^{8}\ \mathrm{K}$ and very high pressure or density. At this temperature the fuel is a plasma that no solid container can hold; it must be confined by magnetic fields, and it is very hard to keep it stable long enough. So far, no experiment produces more usable energy than is supplied to heat and confine the plasma, and there is no commercial fusion reactor.

**Fission** takes place at a modest temperature: a slow neutron splits a uranium-235 nucleus, releasing more neutrons that continue a chain reaction. The reaction is already controllable (the control rods absorb neutrons and the moderator slows them down), the fuel is available, and the technology exists and is proved, so fission reactors already supply a large share of the world's electricity.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State the meaning of acid rain.

(ii) Explain how acid rain is formed and outline two of its adverse effects *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Acid rain** is rain (or other precipitation) that is more acidic than normal rain, that is with a pH below about $5.6$, because it contains dissolved sulphuric and nitric acids.

(ii) **Formation.** Burning fossil fuels that contain sulphur (coal, oil) and the high temperature in engines release sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into the air:
$$\mathrm{S + O_2 \to SO_2}\qquad\qquad \mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \to 2NO}\ \text{(at high temperature)}$$
In the atmosphere these gases are oxidised, for example $\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 \to 2SO_3}$ and $\mathrm{2NO + O_2 \to 2NO_2}$, and dissolve in the water droplets of clouds:
$$\mathrm{SO_3 + H_2O \to H_2SO_4}\qquad\qquad \mathrm{4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \to 4HNO_3}$$
The acid droplets fall as acid rain.

**Two adverse effects:** (1) it acidifies lakes and rivers and kills fish and other aquatic life, and it leaches nutrients from the soil and damages forests and crops; (2) it corrodes buildings, statues and metal structures (it reacts with limestone and marble, $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 \to CaSO_4 + H_2O + CO_2}$, and with iron).
